question: How can one pianist make a melody sound independent of thick chords?
intro: A long melody presses through repeated chords; a quieter cantabile passage changes the balance between line and accompaniment. Follow the opening’s enlarged return and the retreat into a major-key close.

cues.title: A melody through chords
cues.text: The opening marks the melody “molto marcato” — strongly projected — above repeated chords. Listen for the long notes as a connected line, distinct from the more frequent attacks underneath them.
cues.evidence: The inspected piano score, printed p. 63, shows Appassionato and molto marcato, with sustained melody above chordal triplets: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f5/IMSLP39591-PMLP01894-Rachmaninoff-Etudes-Op39.pdf. The analysis records an active opening; this note does not time a particular note.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Before leaving Russia
cues.text: Rachmaninoff composed the Op. 39 collection in 1916–17. He left Russia with his family later in 1917 and never returned; these studies belong to the final phase of his Russian career, not his later American concert years.
cues.evidence: IMSLP dates the collection 1916–17. Nigel Simeone’s Phillips Collection programme note places it before Rachmaninoff’s permanent departure: https://www.phillipscollection.org/event/2016-11-12-vadym-kholodenko-0

cues.title: Another kind of accompaniment
cues.text: In the contrasting passage, follow the more continuously moving accompaniment beneath the singing line. The difference is not simply loud versus soft: repeated blocks give way to notes spread through the harmony.
cues.evidence: Printed score pp. 65–66 replaces the chordal accompaniment with flowing broken chords. The analysis has a boundary at 1:02 and quieter windows at 1:00–1:05, followed by further changes at 1:14 and 1:24. Placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hear through the accidentals
cues.text: Through the central passage, listen for small steps within the moving harmony. A note can remain in place while another shifts by a semitone; the changing chord does not always require a new melodic idea.
cues.evidence: Printed score pp. 66–67 contains chromatic voice-leading within the broken-chord texture. The analysis shows unstable key estimates here; those estimates are not used to name individual chords or modulation points.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Nine study pictures
cues.text: Op. 39 contains nine solo-piano études, published in 1917 by Edition Russe. “Étude-tableau” combines a technical study with a picture; the fifth piece’s printed heading gives a tempo and character, not the name of a painted scene.
cues.evidence: IMSLP lists nine pieces, publication in 1917 and Edition Russe plates 333–341: https://imslp.org/wiki/Etudes-tableaux,_Op.39_(Rachmaninoff,_Sergei). The inspected fifth étude is headed Appassionato, without a pictorial programme.

cues.title: The opening with more weight
cues.text: In the later expansion, recognise the opening’s broad line beneath the denser chordal writing. Returning material changes register and weight: recognition depends on its contour, not on a literal copy of the first texture.
cues.evidence: Printed score pp. 68–69 restores the opening material under Tempo I and pesante, with the melody projected in the lower part. The report places the strongest sustained level region around 2:20–2:50; the estimated return boundary is not a checked bar onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Beyond the largest crest
cues.text: After the main accumulation, listen for the reduction in chordal weight. The score restores a more flowing accompaniment and then a sustained singing line; the closing passage does not need to outdo the loudest return.
cues.evidence: Printed score pp. 69–70 moves from fortissimo chordal writing to a quieter broken-chord texture. Analysis boundaries at 3:14 and 3:28 accompany a decline from roughly −9 dB near 2:45 to −25.3 at 3:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gilanyan and Musopen
cues.text: Karine Gilanyan is the pianist in this Musopen recording. Commons dates the performance only to 2005–07; its December 2007 upload is not a more precise recording date.
cues.evidence: The Commons description names Karine Gilanyan, links Musopen and supplies the range “between 2005 and 2007”; file history gives the separate upload date: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sergei_Rachmaninoff_-_Etudes-Tableaux,_Op._39,_No._5.oga

cues.title: The minor key releases
cues.text: The ending settles into E♭ major and dies away. Listen to the last broken chords as resonance beneath the remaining upper notes: the work that begins with strongly projected melody finishes by reducing its weight.
cues.evidence: The final score page, printed p. 71, supplies E♭-major harmony and morendo. The report corroborates E♭-major pitch content and declining level from 4:00 through 4:20; near-silence occupies the last seconds of the 4:31 file.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Repeated blocks open into broken chords
transitions.how: The forceful opening phrase recedes, and the accompaniment changes from reiterated chords to a continuous broken-chord figure. Longer melodic notes remain above it. The join changes how the harmony is distributed in time: instead of striking much of a chord together, Rachmaninoff lets its notes pass beneath the line, creating space for the quieter cantabile passage.
transitions.evidence: Printed score p. 65 shows the quiet melody above the new broken-chord figure. The 1:02 analysis boundary and the dip from −9.4 dB at 0:50 to −23.6 at 1:05 anchor an approximate change of texture.

transitions.title: The opening presses through new chords
transitions.how: The central writing accumulates chordal force through a written acceleration and crescendo, then broadens with a ritenuto. Tempo I and pesante recover the opening material, now with greater weight in the lower voice beneath repeated upper chords. Rachmaninoff makes the return a redistribution of the melody as well as a recovery of its notes.
transitions.evidence: Printed score pp. 67–68 contains accelerando, crescendo, ritenuto, Tempo I and pesante. The report shows high activity and level across 2:20–2:50 and a boundary at 2:24; this is an approximate return region, not an exact score alignment.

transitions.title: Chordal pressure becomes a singing close
transitions.how: The repeated chords give way to a flowing accompaniment and a quieter melodic continuation. The closing music revisits the cantabile manner rather than adding a new climax. As it settles, E♭ major replaces the minor-key tension; the final morendo asks the sound to die away while the broken chords still sustain the harmony.
transitions.evidence: Printed score pp. 69–71 shows the quieter accompaniment, cantabile continuation and E♭-major morendo ending. A 3:14 boundary and substantial level reduction across 3:15–3:25 support the provisional coda position.

composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
facts: Moscow Conservatory: piano with Nikolai Zverev and Alexander Siloti; counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev, composition with Anton Arensky
Mamontov’s Moscow Private Russian Opera, 1897–98 · Bolshoi Theatre, 1904–06
Ivanovka near Tambov · Dresden · New York · Villa Senar, Lake Lucerne · Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
